title: Modular Code
author: Barbara Vreede, Ole Mussmann
plainText:
--- title: Modular Code type: slides order: 2 author: Barbara Vreede, Ole Mussmann description: Modular coding --- # Developing Modular Code === ## What is modularity? Simple components combined to produce complex behavior. - Software can be 'built up' from smaller elements. - Elements are self-contained and independent. - Each element handles a specific (set of) task(s). === ## Modular code
=== ## What are these blocks/elements?
  • functions
  • classes
  • modules
  • libraries/packages
  • programs
  • ...
=== ## Why write modular code? To increase robustness - A well-designed module can be tested. - This helps keep the codebase well-functioning and bug-free. === ## Why write modular code? To make maintenance easier: - Modular code is more readable and understandable. - Modules can be debugged separately. - Modules only need to be improved/optimized once. === ## Why write modular code? To allow reusability: - A module can live independent of its original context. - It can be reused by another project. === ## Why write modular code? To facilitate scalability:
  • Complexity remains low by design.
  • This creates space for scaling up.
=== ## Why write modular code? To create opportunities for innovation: - Modules increase the capabilities and power of a project. - Rearrange old modules for new applications. === ## Why write modular code? To save time: === ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
=== ## Naming your module - be descriptive and clear - focus on human intelligibility - follow language specific conventions - avoid abbreviations
=== ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
  • is readable
=== ## More readable != shorter code Shorter: ```python indexATG = [n for n,i in enumerate(myList) if i == 'ATG'] indexAAG = [n for n,i in enumerate(myList) if i == 'AAG'] ``` More modular: ```python def getIndex(inputList,z): zIndex = [n for n,i in enumerate(inputList) if i == z] return zIndex indexATG = getIndex(myList,'ATG') indexAAG = getIndex(myList,'AAG') ``` === ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
  • is readable
  • is pure and predictable
=== ## An impure function... ... does not always give the same result: ```python def fahrenheit_to_celsius(temp_list, converted_temps=[]): for temp in temp_list: temp_c = (temp - 32.0) * (5.0/9.0) converted_temps.append(temp_c) return converted_temps >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0] ``` **Q: What will happen when we call the function a second time?** ```python >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0, 0.0, 25.0] ``` === ## A pure function... ... always gives the same result: ```python def fahrenheit_to_celsius(temp_list, converted_temps=None): if converted_temps == None: converted_temps = [] for temp in temp_list: temp_c = (temp - 32.0) * (5.0/9.0) converted_temps.append(temp_c) return converted_temps >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0] >>> fahrenheit_to_celsius([32.0, 77.0]) # [0.0, 25.0] ``` === ## A good module...
  • performs limited and clearly defined tasks
  • has a good name
  • is readable
  • is pure and predictable
=== ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
=== ## Readable code Modular code becomes more readable - Code is read more than it is written - Does a reader understand what the code does? - Bad readability can be a "code smell" === ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
  • repetition
=== ## Repetitive code - Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY): place reused code into a function - Identify functions units by their _action_ - (e.g. "plot", "transform", "extract", "save")
=== ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
  • repetition
  • nested code
=== ## Target nested code Nested code is a prime target for modularization: ```python def sum_even_numbers(bottom, top): if top > bottom: sum = 0 for x in range(bottom, top): if x % 2 == 0: sum += x return sum return 0 sum_even_numbers(2, 14) # 42 ``` === ## Reduce nestedness... ... by extracting modules: ```python def _filter_even(number): if number % 2 == 0: return number return 0 def sum_even_numbers(bottom, top): if top < bottom: return 0 sum = 0 for x in range(bottom, top): sum += _filter_even(x) return sum sum_even_numbers (2,14) # 42 ``` === ## Identifying opportunities for modularization
  • poor readability
  • repetition
  • nested code
=== ## Let tests help you - Write tests for each individual module - Use the test-writing procedure to look critically at the module's function: - Is the input/output clear? - What can you not yet test? Extract it into a new module.

title: Collaborative Development
description: Section 4: Software Development as a Process
author: Sander van Rijn
plainText:
--- title: Collaborative Development type: slides order: 5 author: Sander van Rijn description: "Section 4: Software Development as a Process" --- # Collaborative Software Development for Reuse === ## Collaborative Software Development for Reuse - Code Review - Improving the quality of code - Detecting bugs and code defects early - Increasing knowledge of the software within the team - Preparing Software for Reuse - Documentation - `pyproject.toml` file - Citation file - License - Packaging Software for Release == ## Collaborative Code Development Models - Shared Repository Model -> collaborators all work in a single repository - Fork and Pull Model -> external contributions from forked repositories When to use which model? Note: In this episode you'll learn how to work together using code review. This can be done in several ways, but we'll show you the most common way this is done in large organizations and in most open source projects: using the fork and pull method. === ## Developing Software in a Team: Code Review Note: Here's a schematic overview of the Fork & Pull method: It should remind you of a git workflow with feature branches. In principle, that's exactly what this is. To Fork a repository means to make a personal copy of a repository in your account. Note that this is a account action which maintains the link between the repository on your account and the original one. You can use the fork to create your feature branches for whatever changes you want to make. But instead of directly merging, you have to make a request to the original repository to accept your merge. In GitHub terms this is called a Pull Request (PR), as you're asking them to pull your changes into their repository. On GitLab, this same process is called a Merge Request (MR). The PR is again a GitHub specific thing, which creates a place to view the proposed changes and discuss them. Any future pushed commits to the branch for which you've made the PR, will automatically update the PR. == ## Real World example https://github.com/TUDelftGeodesy/sarxarray/pull/67/ == ## Code Documentation Probably the most underappreciated but most important skill of good software engineering practices. If I spend some time now on documenting my code well, this will save me time and headaches later. Note: Another important part of online collaboration and preparing your code for reuse and release is to create a good README. This is the billboard for your repository and is shown as your 'homepage' on GitHub. There are several best practices of what should be included in a README, which you will learn about in this episode. Documentation does not only help others, but also yourself: if you work on other projects and come back later, you will have forgotten most of the details. === ## Types of Documentation - README file - In-code documentation and Docstrings - User documentation - Tutorials - ... === ## A good README - A descriptive project title - Motivation (why the project exists) and basics - Installation / How to setup - Badges - Contributing guidelines - ... Examples: - https://github.com/numpy/numpy - https://github.com/pydata/xarray === ## In code documentations Do not use it: - When the code is self-explanatory - To replace good variable/function names - To replace version control - To keep old (zombie) code around == ### Commented Code ```python # convert from degrees celcius to fahrenheit as def convert(d): return d * 5 / 9 + 32 ``` ### Readable Code ```python def celcius_to_fahrenheit(degrees: float) -> float: return degrees * 5 / 9 + 32 ``` == ### Keeping Zombie Code ```python # Do not run this code!: # if temperature > 0: # print("It is warm") ``` ### Replacing Git ```python # removed on August 5 # if ... # Now it connects to the API with o-auth2, updated 2026-05-05 ``` == ## Docstrings: a special kind of comment 

def celcius_to_fahrenheit(degrees: float) -> float:
    """Convert degrees Celcius to degrees Fahrenheit.

    Parameters
    ----------
    degrees : float
        Temperature in degrees Celcius.

    Returns
    -------
    float
        Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit.
    """
    return degrees * 5 / 9 + 32
VSCode plugins like autoDocstring can help you generate docstrings!
Note: Plugin URL: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=njpwerner.autodocstring === ## User Documentation Options include _MKDocs_ (Zensical) and Sphinx Note: Urls: - MKDocs https://www.mkdocs.org - Typically used with Material for MKDocs https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/ - EOL as of 2027-05-05 - Zensical (standalone (Material for) MKDocs successor) https://zensical.org - Sphinx: https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/index.html - To use with markdown, include the MyST Parser extension https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/markdown.html#markdown ===
